summary: Registers the message/sipfrag media type, which is like message/sip but can carry well-formed pieces of a SIP message instead of a complete one. It is used for end-to-end security purposes and with the REFER method to report the status of a referenced request.

plainLanguage.summary: A SIP message is like a letter. Sometimes you only want to quote part of it. This note creates a label for envelopes that hold just a piece of such a letter.

questions: what is the sipfrag media type
how does sip refer report status
what is a sip message fragment
subtitle: A MIME type for carrying a piece of a SIP message instead of the whole thing.

tldr.problem: The message/sip media type can only carry a complete SIP message, but some uses need to carry or protect just part of one.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3420 registers message/sipfrag, which is any valid SIP message with some of the start line, header fields or body deleted.
tldr.outcome: It is used for end-to-end security assertions and with the REFER method to report the status of a referenced request without exposing the whole message.

today: RFC 3420 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2002, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Fragment Type
sections.content:
The message/sip media type carries an entire, well-formed SIP message. It is used together with S/MIME for end-to-end security. The same idea can be extended so a SIP entity can make assertions about a subset of a message, and the new message/sipfrag type represents that subset.

The REFER method also uses a subset of a SIP message to carry the status of a referenced request. Sending only a portion lets information that could harm privacy and confidentiality be removed.

The RFC does not provide a way to cut a SIP message into pieces for separate transport and reassemble it. That job belongs to the message/partial type from RFC 2046.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you only want to share part of a letter, like one line, and keep the rest private. This gives you a way to do that.

sections.title: Definition of message/sipfrag
sections.content:
A valid message/sipfrag part is one you could get by starting from a valid SIP message and deleting any of these: the entire start line, one or more entire header fields, or the body.

The grammar, in ABNF, is sipfrag = [ start-line ] *message-header [ CRLF [ message-body ] ], using the SIP grammar elements. Every element is still subject to the restrictions on valid SIP messages.

If a part contains a body, it MUST also contain the header fields that describe that body (such as Content-Length) and the empty line that separates headers from the body.
sections.plainLanguage: You take a full message and cross out whole lines, such as the first line, some header lines, or the main text. What is left is a fragment.

sections.title: Valid and Invalid Fragments
sections.content:
The RFC shows that a fragment can be just a start line, such as SIP/2.0 603 Declined. It can be a few headers after a start line, or headers with no start line at all, which suits a part that might be signed to make assertions about a message. It can also contain a body, as long as the needed headers come with it.

Invalid fragments break the normal SIP rules. A start line that is present must be complete and valid, so a bare INVITE or SIP/2.0 is not allowed. Every header field must be valid, so a malformed To, a bad Call-ID or a duplicated tag parameter makes the part invalid. A body with no required headers and no empty line separator is invalid too.
sections.plainLanguage: You may show any piece of the letter, but whatever lines you show must still be written correctly. A half-written line is not allowed.

sections.title: Why Fragments Help
sections.content:
With message/sipfrag and S/MIME, a sender can protect and make assertions about portions of a SIP message header. Applications can also describe the messaging in a SIP transaction using parts of the messages themselves.

For REFER, including the whole response as message/sip is rarely desirable and has significant negative security implications. A fragment lets the sender choose what to expose and leave out header fields that do not matter, which also reduces size. For example, an element can report a 400 Bad Request with its Warning header field without including the Via, To, From, Call-ID, CSeq and Content-Length headers.

Protecting a whole message is awkward because some header fields change in transit. Protecting only a subset avoids the work and possible mistakes of ignoring parts that may legitimately change.
sections.plainLanguage: Showing the whole letter might give away secrets. Showing only the useful lines keeps private things hidden and the envelope smaller.

sections.title: The Registration
sections.content:
The registered media type is message with subtype sipfrag. It has no required parameters and one optional parameter, version, which is the SIP-Version number of the enclosed message such as 2.0. If it is absent, the version defaults to 2.0.

SIP messages must be treated as binary, since they have an 8-bit header optionally followed by a binary MIME data object. Normally they travel over binary-capable transports, so no special encoding is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the official name tag for the new envelope, with an optional note saying which SIP version the piece came from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A fragment may hold sensitive information or information that affects how a receiver processes it. When exposing or altering it in transit would do harm, protection can be improved with the S/MIME mechanisms of the SIP specification (section 23, with the limitations in its section 26) and with the mechanisms in the authenticated identity draft.

Applications must also consider that a fragment could be captured and replayed, and must include enough information to reduce that risk. Any SIP extension that uses message/sipfrag MUST describe the replay and cut-and-paste threats specific to its use.
sections.plainLanguage: A piece of a letter could be copied and shown somewhere else. Anyone using these pieces has to think about how to stop that trick.
